standard.title: Significant Events, Ideas and Movements — Federation and Australian Democracy
standard.description: significant events, ideas, people, groups and movements in the development of Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify significant events and describe the roles of individuals and groups in historical change (AC9HH8K05, AC9HH8K10, AC9HH8K15). They have not yet examined the specific factors driving Australian Federation, the constitutional process, the development of Australian democratic institutions, or the role of women's suffrage in Australian democracy.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the rise of nationalist sentiment in Australia, explain the factors contributing to Federation and the development of democracy, describe the key steps to Federation, examine influences on the Australian Constitution, analyse the significance of women's voting rights, and investigate key people and groups in the Federation movement.

nodes.label: The rise of Australian nationalism and the case for Federation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the rise of nationalist sentiment in Australia in the late 19th century and explain the main factors that made Federation appealing to colonial leaders and populations.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe Australian nationalist sentiment as a growing sense of shared identity distinct from Britain, and identify at least three factors driving Federation (e.g. defence, economic integration, White Australia sentiment, egalitarian nationalism).
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the development of a distinct Australian identity through the 1880s–90s — the Bulletin, bush mythology, sport, the labour movement; the specific arguments for Federation — defence against potential threats (Russia, Germany, Japan), economic arguments (tariff barriers between colonies, unified rail gauge, single currency), the 1890s depression as a catalyst; the 'White Australia' ideal as a shared motivation across colonies despite different interests; the role of the labour movement and egalitarian values in shaping the Federation vision.
wider: Examine the cultural construction of Australian identity in the 1880s–90s through The Bulletin, bush poets and painters — analysing what identity was being projected and whose experience it reflected
Evaluate which factor was most significant in driving Federation — defence, economics, or identity — developing a supported position
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding why Federation was sought is prerequisite for understanding the constitutional process (N2). Students who see Federation as inevitable rather than as a response to specific pressures cannot explain why it took the form it did, why some colonies were reluctant, or why the Constitution reflects particular compromises.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat Federation as the natural outcome of being Australian rather than as a negotiated political project with specific motivations. Making the factors explicit — and their relative weight contestable — is the scaffold for understanding constitutional compromises in N2.

success_criteria: Describes the rise of Australian nationalist sentiment in the late 19th century
Identifies and explains at least three factors that contributed to the push for Federation

nodes.label: The Federation process — key steps and constitutional influences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the key steps in the Federation process and examine the influences on the development of the Australian Constitution.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the main steps (at least three: conventions, referenda, Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act) and identify two influences on the Constitution (British Westminster system and American federalism).
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the Federation conference and convention sequence; the role of key figures (Parkes, Griffith, Deakin); the two referenda on the draft Constitution and why the first failed; the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900; examine the Westminster inheritance (responsible government, cabinet system, Parliament) and the American influence (federal structure, Senate with equal state representation, separation of powers); explain what each model contributed and what compromises were made between large and small colonies.
wider: Examine a specific constitutional compromise — e.g. Senate equal-state representation vs House of Representatives proportional representation — and explain what interests it served and what it sacrificed
Investigate why Western Australia was the last colony to vote for Federation and what its late adhesion reveals about the limits of Federation's appeal

response_modes.reason: The Federation process involves a specific sequence of events and institutions that students need to know accurately. Common errors — confusing the conventions with the referenda, misidentifying which system influenced which part of the Constitution — are precision errors worth targeted practice.

success_criteria: Describes at least three key steps in the Federation process in correct sequence
Identifies two constitutional influences and explains what each contributed to the Australian Constitution

nodes.label: Women's suffrage and the development of Australian democracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the significance of the advance of women's voting rights in Australia, including the suffragist movement, and describe how Australian women's suffrage compared to other democracies.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the achievement of women's suffrage in Australia (Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902), name at least one key suffragist figure or movement, and explain why this was significant for Australian democracy.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the suffragist movements in colonial and then federal Australia; the role of specific figures (Catherine Helen Spence, Vida Goldstein, Muriel Matters) and organisations (Christian Women's Temperance Union, Women's Suffrage League); the arguments made for and against women's suffrage; the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 as making Australian women among the first in the world to gain the federal vote; the significant exclusion — First Nations Australians remained disenfranchised; evaluate what women's suffrage meant for Australian democracy both as an achievement and as a limited one.
wider: Compare Australian women's suffrage with the suffrage movements in Britain and the USA — examining why Australia achieved it earlier and what difference the colonial/dominion context made
Examine the exclusion of First Nations Australians from the Commonwealth Franchise — analysing what this reveals about whose democracy Federation created and for whom
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The exclusion of First Nations Australians from the franchise alongside the inclusion of women creates a genuinely complex democratic story — one that resists simple celebration. The comparative question (why earlier than Britain?) demands historical analysis about the conditions that made early suffrage possible.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly frame women's suffrage as a simple victory without examining its limits (First Nations exclusion) or its international context. Multiple perspectives — suffragists, opponents, First Nations Australians, British suffragists — build the fuller picture.

success_criteria: Describes the achievement of women's suffrage in Australia with at least one key figure or movement
Explains the significance of women's suffrage for Australian democracy, including both its achievement and its limits
